commits.pr_title: [Perf][Kernel] Vectorized flat abs-max for dynamic per-tensor FP8 quantization
commits.pr_body:
## Purpose

This PR speeds up the abs-max pass of `dynamic_scaled_fp8_quant` (per-tensor dynamic FP8 quantization) in `csrc/libtorch_stable/quantization/w8a8/fp8/common.cu`. It is the activation quant on every MoE layer of a model served with `--quantization fp8`, and it had never been performance-tuned.

I went in after reading #44173, which took the same kind of kernel (block-per-row, shared-memory tree reduction, scalar loads) and rewrote it as warp shuffles plus vector loads. This kernel had the same shape of problem, so I applied the same approach and measured what it actually buys.

**What was there before**

`segmented_max_reduction_strided` launched one block per token, did one scalar load per element, reduced through a 256-entry shared-memory tree with a `__syncthreads` per level, and issued one atomic per token. For a decode batch of 32 tokens, that is 32 blocks on a 132-SM GPU. For a 65536-token prefill it is 65536 atomics to one address.

**What this PR does**

- For contiguous input, the abs-max is a flat grid-stride kernel over 16-element vectors (32 B loads for bf16, 64 B for fp32). The reduction is a `__shfl_xor_sync` butterfly within each warp and one shared-memory exchange across warps, so a single barrier. The grid is sized from the vector count and capped at 8 blocks per SM, so a small batch gets exactly the blocks it needs and a large one loops. One atomic per block instead of one per token.
- Strided or unaligned input keeps the one-block-per-token kernel, now with vectorized loads (`vectorize_read_with_alignment`) and the same shuffle reduction in place of the tree.
- The quantize pass that follows is unchanged.

**Numerics**

Output is bit-for-bit identical to `main`. The per-element operations are unchanged (`fmaxf` for the abs-max, the same `scaled_fp8_conversion` for the quantize). `fmaxf` is order-invariant, and dividing by a positive constant is monotonic, so regrouping the max across threads, warps, or blocks cannot change any scale or any output byte. I verified this empirically rather than relying on the argument; see below. No API change. Strided rows and all dtypes behave as before.

**Not a duplicate.** #41115 (open since May, merge conflicts, no review) tunes block sizes on the per-token kernel and does not touch the per-tensor path. #55330 targets the per-token-group kernel and #45428 the fused RMSNorm quant kernel.

**Next work.** Once this is approved and merged, I plan a follow-up PR for the per-token kernel in the same file, which reuses the reduction helpers added here.

## Test Plan

- **Bitwise equivalence.** Built `main` and this branch on the same box. Dumped the quantized bytes and scales on CPU-seeded inputs for bf16 and fp32, M in {1, 7, 64, 512, 4096, 16384}, hidden in {17, 1024, 1025, 2048, 4096, 5137, 7168, 8192, 16384, 32768}, and three row layouts (contiguous, misaligned by 8 elements, aligned but padded by 16). Compared with `torch.equal`.
- **Unit tests.** `tests/kernels/quantization/test_fp8_quant.py`, plus a new strided-input test that forces the fallback kernel at both alignments.
- **Performance.** H100 80 GB HBM3, driver 580, CUDA 13.0.3, torch 2.13.0+cu130. `triton.testing.do_bench_cudagraph`, median of the full op including the memset and both kernels, so this is what a caller sees.
- **End to end.** Qwen3-30B-A3B with `--quantization fp8`, `vllm bench throughput` and `vllm bench latency`, main vs this branch on the same box.

Commands run:

```bash
pre-commit run --files csrc/libtorch_stable/quantization/w8a8/fp8/common.cu tests/kernels/quantization/test_fp8_quant.py
pre-commit run mypy-3.12 --all-files --hook-stage manual
pytest tests/kernels/quantization/test_fp8_quant.py -q
vllm bench throughput --model Qwen/Qwen3-30B-A3B --quantization fp8 --max-model-len 2048 --dataset-name random --input-len 1024 --output-len 128 --num-prompts 512
vllm bench latency --model Qwen/Qwen3-30B-A3B --quantization fp8 --max-model-len 2048 --input-len 1024 --output-len 128 --batch-size 32 --num-iters 10
```

## Test Result

- Bitwise: **1080 cases identical, 0 mismatched**, bytes and scales.
- Tests: **249 passed**.

**Per-tensor, bf16, `main` vs this PR**

| M | hidden | main (us) | PR (us) | speedup |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 16 | 4096 | 8.21 | 5.61 | 1.46x |
| 16 | 8192 | 11.36 | 6.01 | 1.89x |
| 512 | 4096 | 9.58 | 7.39 | 1.30x |
| 512 | 7168 | 12.60 | 8.79 | 1.43x |
| 4096 | 4096 | 48.95 | 30.51 | 1.60x |
| 4096 | 7168 | 85.17 | 55.27 | 1.54x |
| 16384 | 4096 | 187.22 | 115.96 | 1.61x |
| 16384 | 7168 | 312.94 | 196.30 | 1.59x |
| 65536 | 4096 | 715.88 | 436.15 | 1.64x |
| 65536 | 8192 | 1378.42 | 866.10 | 1.59x |

Geomean **1.39x** across bf16 and fp32, M in {16, 512, 4096, 16384, 65536}, hidden in {2048, 4096, 7168, 8192}. Range 1.11x to 1.89x. At large M, the op now moves about 3.0 TB/s of real traffic (two reads and one write), which is where it should sit on this GPU.

**End to end: Qwen3-30B-A3B with online FP8**

`--quantization fp8` quantizes activations per-tensor dynamically, and on a MoE model, the expert input of every layer goes through this kernel. Same H100, `vllm bench throughput`, random dataset, 1024 in / 128 out, 512 prompts, three interleaved runs per build after a warm compile cache:

| build | tokens/s (3 runs) | mean | stdev |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| main | 43793, 43706, 43835 | 43778 | 66 |
| this PR | 45154, 44810, 44965 | 44977 | 172 |

**+2.7% throughput**, with run-to-run spread under 0.4%. Batch latency (`vllm bench latency`, batch 32, 1024 in / 128 out): 1.876 s vs 1.843 s avg, about 1.8% lower.

The gain lands where expected: with the compiler fusing this model's per-token quant sites into RMSNorm, the per-tensor abs-max pass on the MoE expert inputs is the only kernel this PR changes that runs in the trace. Model output is unaffected since the kernel is bitwise identical.

I used Claude Code for this change. I reviewed every line and ran the tests and benchmarks above myself.

---

<details>
<summary>Essential Elements of an Effective PR Description Checklist</summary>

- [x] The purpose of the PR (performance; bitwise-identical output).
- [x] The test plan (bitwise-equivalence dump, unit tests, perf sweep, end-to-end).
- [x] The test results (identical bytes and scales; tests pass; H100 tables).
- [x] (Optional) Documentation update: n/a, no API or behavior change.

</details>

commits.pr_title: [Kernel][Perf] Register-resident path for per-token-group 8-bit quant
commits.pr_body:
## Summary

`per_token_group_quant_8bit` stages every group through shared memory because it
reads the group twice: once to reduce absmax, once to quantize. At `group_size`
128 a group of 16-bit input is 256 B, which fits in registers, so both the
staging and the `__syncthreads()` separating the two passes are avoidable.

This adds `per_token_group_quant_8bit_register_kernel` for the unpacked float32
scale layout. It is taken when `group_size == 128`, the input is 16-bit, both
buffers are 16 B aligned, and both are contiguous; everything else keeps the
existing shared-memory schedule.

vLLM already has `per_token_group_quant_8bit_packed_register_kernel` with the
same register pipeline, but float32-scale callers cannot reach it: it is
hardwired to UE8M0 exponents packed 4-per-int32 with TMA-aligned strides. Rather
than reshaping those callers, this extends the same idea to the ordinary scale
layout, reusing that kernel's subgroup shuffle mask and UE8M0 exponent bit math
verbatim.

A second, smaller effect of the fixed 256-thread launch: `GetGroupsPerBlock`
falls back to 1 group per block when `num_groups` is odd, leaving 16 active
threads per block. The register path pads the grid and bounds-checks instead, so
it is unaffected — visible below as the `(1, 128)` and `(333, 128)` rows, where
the shared-memory schedule spends ~14 µs almost entirely on launch overhead.

## Not a duplicate

```bash
gh pr list --repo vllm-project/vllm --state open --search "per_token_group_quant"
gh pr list --repo vllm-project/vllm --state open --search "per token group quant register"
```

No open PR touches this kernel's schedule. The nearest work is in different
directions:

- #53874, #54857, #43907 — ROCm/aiter **fusions** (folding the quant into GeGLU,
  RMSNorm, or RoPE), not a schedule change to the CUDA kernel.
- #53346, #51477 — UE8M0 correctness fixes in the Triton paths and in fusion
  eligibility.
- #45151, #36297, #46935 — folding per-group quant into another kernel's
  epilogue (attention, BMM, async-TP).
- #48653 — adds FP8 type dispatch for the transformers backend.

This PR changes only how the existing CUDA kernel is scheduled, and leaves the
kernel that other work fuses into intact.

## Performance

H20-3e (SM90), CUDA 13.0. Microbenchmark against the shipped shared-memory
kernel via `torch.ops._C.per_token_group_fp8_quant` /
`torch.ops._C.per_token_group_quant_int8`, µs per call, output buffers
preallocated so allocation is outside the timed region.

FP8 output, UE8M0 scales (the DeepGEMM default), row-major:

| input dtype | shape | smem | register | speedup |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| bf16 | (1, 128) | 14.0 | 5.5 | 2.54× |
| bf16 | (333, 128) | 13.8 | 5.3 | 2.62× |
| bf16 | (1024, 6144) | 24.2 | 9.1 | 2.66× |
| bf16 | (8192, 6144) | 183.9 | 59.9 | 3.07× |
| bf16 | (65536, 256) | 62.9 | 22.1 | 2.84× |
| fp16 | (8192, 6144) | 180.3 | 55.5 | 3.25× |
| fp16 | (65536, 256) | 61.8 | 20.7 | 2.99× |

FP8 output across the scale-layout matrix, bf16 input:

| shape | ue8m0 | column-major | smem | register | speedup |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| (8192, 6144) | yes | no | 184.1 | 60.1 | 3.06× |
| (8192, 6144) | yes | yes | 194.2 | 64.0 | 3.03× |
| (8192, 6144) | no | no | 175.0 | 76.7 | 2.28× |
| (8192, 6144) | no | yes | 184.8 | 83.2 | 2.22× |
| (65536, 256) | yes | yes | 66.5 | 23.8 | 2.80× |
| (65536, 256) | no | no | 60.1 | 28.2 | 2.13× |
| (65536, 256) | no | yes | 63.4 | 30.4 | 2.08× |

INT8 output (no UE8M0 scales), bf16 input:

| shape | smem | register | speedup |
|---|---|---|---|
| (1, 128) | 6.7 | 5.1 | 1.32× |
| (333, 128) | 6.6 | 4.9 | 1.36× |
| (1024, 6144) | 14.9 | 11.7 | 1.27× |
| (8192, 6144) | 118.4 | 76.1 | 1.56× |
| (65536, 256) | 40.8 | 27.9 | 1.46× |

The spread is worth explaining rather than quoting the best number. The register
side converges to ~60–77 µs at (8192, 6144) in all three tables — it is
bandwidth-bound. The differences come from the baseline:

- `c10::Float8_e4m3fn(float)` is a software conversion and costs materially more
  than int8's hardware `cvt`, so the FP8 baseline starts slower (175 vs 118 µs)
  and has more to give back.
- On the register side UE8M0 is ~22% faster than float32 scales because a
  power-of-two scale lets the inner loop multiply by the reciprocal instead of
  dividing per element.

So the ~3× on the UE8M0 FP8 path is three effects stacked (no smem round trip,
reciprocal instead of divide, an expensive baseline conversion), not register
residency alone. INT8 keeps a smaller but consistent 1.26–1.56×.

Reproducing:

```bash
python benchmarks/kernels/benchmark_per_token_group_quant.py --dtype fp8
```

Run it on `main` and on this branch and compare the CUDA column (this PR adds
serving-sized shapes to that script's defaults, which previously topped out at
512 groups). The `gs=64` rows do not meet the dispatch condition and should be
unchanged across the two runs, which makes them a useful control.

### End-to-end serving

GLM-5.2-FP8, TP=8 on 8×H20-3e, 256k max model len, chunked prefill at 8192,
concurrency 1, `--kv-cache-dtype fp8`. Same server config and same benchmark
script on both sides, run back to back in one window:

| prompt tokens | baseline | with register path | throughput | latency |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 8192 | 3591.9 tok/s | 3622.5 tok/s | +0.85% | 2.279 → 2.264 s |
| 16384 | 3560.7 tok/s | 3620.9 tok/s | +1.69% | 4.596 → 4.519 s |
| 65536 | 3351.0 tok/s | 3404.3 tok/s | +1.59% | 19.529 → 19.213 s |
| 131072 | 3078.6 tok/s | 3123.9 tok/s | +1.47% | 42.471 → 41.872 s |

The 8k row gains least because at one chunk the fixed per-request costs (HTTP,
tokenization, scheduling, sampling) are the largest share of wall clock, while
the kernel saving scales with token count. From 16k up it settles at 1.5–1.7%.

That is consistent with the profile attribution: at an 8192-token chunk this
kernel accounts for 22.28 ms per step (15.60 ms over 411 calls with column-major
scales plus 6.68 ms over 150 row-major), and the measured 3.03×/3.07× puts it
near 7.3 ms — about 15 ms off a ~800 ms step, or 1.87% of GPU time. End-to-end
lands slightly under that because the denominator also carries non-GPU work.

Measurement caveat, and it biases against this PR: to avoid rebuilding the
prebuilt `_C_stable_libtorch.abi3.so` in that environment, the served run reached
the kernel through a Python-level redirect of the op call, so every call paid an
extra Python frame and predicate. Built normally the dispatch happens before the
launch, so treat 1.5% as a lower bound. Baseline reproducibility was checked
independently: the back-to-back baseline matched an earlier run from several
hours before to within 0.2% at every length.

## Bit-exactness, and why there are no eval numbers

Output is bit-exact with the shared-memory kernel in every configuration tested
below — quantized bytes and scales compare equal with `torch.equal`, not within
a tolerance. Two details carry that:

- The UE8M0 scale is derived with the same exponent bit math
  (`exp_bits + (mant_bits != 0)`) that `per_token_group_quant_8bit_packed_register_kernel`
  already uses, which is equivalent to `exp2f(ceilf(log2f(...)))` on this input
  domain.
- The non-UE8M0 path divides by the scale instead of multiplying by its
  reciprocal. The reciprocal costs an ulp and moves the ~0.05% of values that
  land exactly on an 8-bit boundary. Only the UE8M0 path, where the scale is a
  power of two and the two are equivalent, multiplies.

Because the bytes are identical, an accuracy eval would reproduce `main`'s
numbers exactly and would not be evidence of anything. I have not run one, and
am offering the bit-exactness comparison in its place. Happy to run a specific
eval if a reviewer would rather see it.

## Testing

Extended the existing suite rather than adding a file. `test_per_token_group_quant_fp8`
gained `dtype` parametrization (bf16/fp16) and three shapes that exercise the new
schedule: a single group, an odd token count leaving a partial trailing block,
and a serving-sized shape.

Its assertions are `atol=0.15` against Triton, which cannot see a bit-level
difference, so two dedicated tests pin the path equivalence. Both build a
16 B-misaligned but contiguous input, which falls back to the shared-memory
schedule, and require the two paths to agree exactly:

- `test_per_token_group_quant_fp8_register_matches_smem` (24 cases)
- `test_per_token_group_quant_int8_register_matches_smem` (6 cases) — int8 shares
  the schedule via `per_token_group_quant_int8`, and differs from fp8 in how
  `DST_DTYPE(q)` rounds (truncation toward zero vs round-to-nearest-even), so it
  needs its own guard.

```bash
pytest tests/kernels/quantization/test_per_token_group_quant.py \
    -k "register_matches_smem"
# 30 passed in 5.30s

pytest tests/kernels/quantization/test_per_token_group_quant.py \
    -k "test_per_token_group_quant_fp8 and not packed and not register_matches"
# 256 passed in 8.20s
```

Kernel-level bit-exactness was measured separately, since the installed vLLM in
my test container does not carry this patch: the new kernel was compiled into a
standalone extension and compared byte-for-byte against
`torch.ops._C.per_token_group_fp8_quant`, with a profiler check confirming the
baseline really executes `per_token_group_quant_8bit_kernel<c10::BFloat16,
c10::Float8_e4m3fn, false, true, float>` rather than falling back to Triton.

- FP8: 72/72 configurations bit-exact across input dtype, UE8M0, column-major,
  and shape
- INT8: 10/10 bit-exact
- 48/48 bit-exact driven through the `per_token_group_quant_fp8` entry point
  itself, which adds `tma_aligned_scales=True` coverage (input dtype ×
  column-major × TMA alignment × UE8M0 × 4 shapes)
- Edge inputs (all-`+inf`, all-`-inf`, `NaN`, all-zero, 1e-30, 1e30): identical
  bytes on both paths

`nvcc -arch=sm_90a` compiles the modified translation unit clean, and
`pre-commit run --files <the three files>` passes.

## Validation gaps

Stating these rather than implying full coverage:

- **ROCm is untested by me.** The `USE_ROCM` shuffle branch is copied verbatim
  from `per_token_group_quant_8bit_packed_register_kernel` in the same file, so
  it is an already-shipped pattern rather than new code, but I have no AMD
  hardware to confirm it.
- **INT8 has no end-to-end number**, only the microbenchmark above. The serving
  measurement is FP8, which is what GLM-5.2 and the other block-quantized models
  use.
- The served run reached the kernel through a Python-level redirect rather than a
  full rebuild, as noted under performance. The 48-configuration check above was
  run with that redirect active, so the measured run was numerically identical to
  baseline.

## AI assistance

AI assistance (Kiro) was used for this change, recorded as an `Assisted-by:`
trailer on the commit. I have reviewed every changed line, and ran the compile,
tests, microbenchmarks, and profiling described above myself.

commits.pr_title: [Pooling] Preserve reranker tokenization with document limits
commits.pr_body:
## Purpose

For non-separator rerankers, a positive `max_tokens_per_doc` could change the prompt and score even when it didn't truncate the document. This limits the document first, then tokenizes the combined prompt once. Separator-based rerankers are unchanged.

## Reproducer

```bash
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER=1 .venv/bin/python - <<'PY'
from vllm import LLM, PoolingParams

llm = LLM(
    model="tomaarsen/Qwen3-Reranker-0.6B-seq-cls",
    runner="pooling",
    dtype="half",
    seed=17,
    trust_remote_code=True,
    hf_overrides={"use_sep_token": False},
    enforce_eager=True,
    max_model_len=128,
    max_num_batched_tokens=128,
    gpu_memory_utilization=0.25,
)
try:
    for name, limit in (("uncapped", None), ("nonbinding_100", 100)):
        extra = None if limit is None else {"max_tokens_per_doc": limit}
        out = llm.score(
            "alpha ",
            "beta gamma delta epsilon",
            pooling_params=PoolingParams(use_activation=False, extra_kwargs=extra),
            tokenization_kwargs={"add_special_tokens": False},
            use_tqdm=False,
        )[0]
        print(f"{name}: ids={list(out.prompt_token_ids)} raw={out.outputs.score:.12f}")
finally:
    llm.llm_engine.engine_core.shutdown()
PY
```

## Output on main / on branch

Main: `uncapped: ids=[7141, 13440, 21619, 9477, 31204] tokens=5 raw=-2.060278892517 final=0.113017871976 finite=True`

Main: `nonbinding_100: ids=[7141, 220, 19127, 21619, 9477, 31204] tokens=6 raw=-2.034487962723 final=0.115629188716 finite=True`

Branch: `uncapped: ids=[7141, 13440, 21619, 9477, 31204] tokens=5 raw=-2.060278892517 final=0.113017871976 finite=True`

Branch: `nonbinding_100: ids=[7141, 13440, 21619, 9477, 31204] tokens=5 raw=-2.060278892517 final=0.113017871976 finite=True`

On the branch, the non-binding limit matches the uncapped prompt and score.

## Test Plan

```bash
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=7 HF_HUB_CACHE=/tmp/codex-pr57666-hf-cache \
  HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1 VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER=1 VLLM_LOGGING_LEVEL=ERROR \
  .venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/entrypoints/pooling/scoring/test_cross_encoder_offline.py -q
```

`6 passed, 15 warnings in 14.49s`, including all three SentenceTransformers reference tests.

OpenAI Codex (GPT-6) helped draft the implementation.

commits.pr_title: [Bugfix] Fix generative scoring body cancellation
commits.pr_body:
## Purpose

Competing request-body consumers can hang `/generative_scoring`.  With this PR, `FastAPI` now parses the body before cancellation and load tracking begin to eliminate the hang condition, as it does for other typed-body endpoints. The serving and scoring paths are unchanged.

## Reproducer

A full-ASGI reproducer sends valid JSON in two `http.request` frames, yields control after the first frame, and records every `receive()` caller. This deterministically allows the endpoint body reader and disconnect listener to compete for the stream.

Save the following file as `/tmp/repro_generative_scoring_body_race.py`.

```python
import asyncio
import json

from fastapi import FastAPI, Request
from fastapi.responses import JSONResponse

from vllm.entrypoints.generate.generative_scoring.api_router import router
from vllm.entrypoints.generate.generative_scoring.serving import (
    GenerativeScoringRequest,
    GenerativeScoringResponse,
)
from vllm.entrypoints.serve.engine.protocol import UsageInfo
from vllm.entrypoints.serve.utils.api_utils import (
    load_aware_call,
    with_cancellation,
)


class Handler:
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self.calls = 0

    async def create_generative_scoring(self, request, raw_request):
        self.calls += 1
        return GenerativeScoringResponse(
            model="model",
            data=[],
            usage=UsageInfo(prompt_tokens=0, total_tokens=0),
        )


app = FastAPI()
app.include_router(router)
app.state.serving_generative_scoring = Handler()
app.state.enable_server_load_tracking = False


@app.post("/fixed")
@with_cancellation
@load_aware_call
async def fixed(
    request: GenerativeScoringRequest,
    raw_request: Request,
):
    return JSONResponse({"query": request.query})


async def invoke(path: str) -> None:
    queue: asyncio.Queue[dict] = asyncio.Queue()
    sent: list[dict] = []
    receivers: list[str] = []

    async def receive() -> dict:
        task = asyncio.current_task()
        assert task is not None
        receivers.append(task.get_coro().__qualname__)
        return await queue.get()

    async def send(message: dict) -> None:
        sent.append(message)

    scope = {
        "type": "http",
        "asgi": {"version": "3.0"},
        "http_version": "1.1",
        "method": "POST",
        "scheme": "http",
        "path": path,
        "raw_path": path.encode(),
        "query_string": b"",
        "headers": [(b"content-type", b"application/json")],
        "client": ("127.0.0.1", 12345),
        "server": ("127.0.0.1", 8000),
        "app": app,
    }

    payload = json.dumps(
        {
            "query": "q",
            "items": ["i"],
            "label_token_ids": [1],
        }
    ).encode()
    midpoint = len(payload) // 2

    app_task = asyncio.create_task(app(scope, receive, send))

    # Let the endpoint and disconnect-listener tasks start before delivering
    # the fragmented request body.
    for _ in range(3):
        await asyncio.sleep(0)

    await queue.put(
        {
            "type": "http.request",
            "body": payload[:midpoint],
            "more_body": True,
        }
    )
    await asyncio.sleep(0)
    await queue.put(
        {
            "type": "http.request",
            "body": payload[midpoint:],
            "more_body": False,
        }
    )

    try:
        await asyncio.wait_for(asyncio.shield(app_task), timeout=0.05)
        outcome = "completed"
    except TimeoutError:
        outcome = "hung_after_complete_body"

    statuses = [
        message["status"]
        for message in sent
        if message["type"] == "http.response.start"
    ]

    print(
        f"{path}: outcome={outcome} statuses={statuses} "
        f"handler_calls={app.state.serving_generative_scoring.calls}"
    )
    print(f"{path}: receive_consumers={receivers}")

    app_task.cancel()
    await asyncio.gather(app_task, return_exceptions=True)


async def main() -> None:
    await invoke("/generative_scoring")
    await invoke("/fixed")


asyncio.run(main())

```

Run it as:

```bash
.venv/bin/python /tmp/repro_generative_scoring_body_race.py
```

### Output on main

```text
/generative_scoring: outcome=hung_after_complete_body statuses=[] handler_calls=0
/generative_scoring: receive_consumers=['create_generative_scoring', 'listen_for_disconnect', 'create_generative_scoring', 'listen_for_disconnect']
```

### Output on this branch

```text
/generative_scoring: outcome=completed statuses=[200] handler_calls=1
/generative_scoring: receive_consumers=['FastAPI.__call__', 'FastAPI.__call__', 'listen_for_disconnect']
```

## Test Plan

commits.pr_title: [MRV2] Minor model_runner.py code cleanup
[SpecDecode] Add LiLiCorr drafter
commits.pr_body:
## What changes

Add `LiLiCorrDraftModel` (https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.20530) to the existing MRV2 DFlash path. The exported SGLang head reranks global candidate lattices using target embeddings, full-vocabulary log probabilities, draft hidden states and the normalized last committed target context. Both plain and grouped-convolution checkpoints are supported.

The port reuses DFlash2 convolution layers and extracts its existing candidate walk/cache orchestration into a shared helper. Greedy and probabilistic drafting use the current vLLM sampling and rejection machinery. No new scheduler, attention backend or verification algorithm is introduced. Correlator and convolution projections use the draft quantization configuration except for lattice QKV and the split-factor/fused-edge projections. Those retain floating-point weights and `F.linear`; `factor_input_proj`, `out_head` and `in_head` must be excluded during export. Reduced draft vocabularies are outside this scope.

ModelOpt exclusions use checkpoint-local draft layer numbers, while vLLM assigns global runtime layer numbers to draft attention layers. The quantization config now retains its exported exclusions and adds runtime-index aliases before constructing the draft layers. This lets mixed BF16/NVFP4 variants allocate the correct linear method without changing checkpoint names or attention/KV layer identity.

References: SGLang https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/37462, DSpark https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/46995, DFlash2 https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/52816.

PR has been tested on valid LiLiCorr checkpoint using 4xGB200 GPUs. It has achieved identical AL.

commits.pr_title: [Core] Model console logging as CLI configuration
commits.pr_body:
Addresses #57200.

Adds a typed `LoggingConfig` to `VllmConfig` with three initial fields:

- `configure_logging`
- `log_level`
- `pylogging_config_file`

The complete object can be supplied as `--logging-config` JSON or with dotted arguments such as `--logging-config.log_level DEBUG`. `--log-level` is a convenience override for `log_level`, while the pre-existing `--log-config-file` is retained as a legacy override for `pylogging_config_file`.

The same model is available through serve YAML and Python configuration. `VLLM_CONFIGURE_LOGGING`, `VLLM_LOGGING_LEVEL`, and `VLLM_LOGGING_CONFIG_PATH` remain as compatibility defaults. Explicit CLI and YAML configuration takes precedence, and the convenience/legacy CLI arguments override their matching `--logging-config` fields.

The resolved configuration is applied after argument parsing and propagated through `VllmConfig` to Uvicorn and API, engine, coordinator, and worker processes. This fixes the asymmetry where a CLI-supplied `--log-config-file` configured Uvicorn but arrived too late for vLLM's already-initialized root logger. Code that previously inspected `VLLM_LOGGING_LEVEL` directly now uses the effective logger level.

The existing default text output and custom Python `dictConfig` behavior are preserved. Tests cover JSON and dotted CLI forms, CLI/YAML/environment precedence, post-import reconfiguration, custom configuration files, and spawned-process propagation.

commits.pr_title: [MoE] Defer the TRTLLM-Gen top-k finalize on the modular path
commits.pr_body:
## Purpose

#53152 lets the monolithic TRTLLM-Gen experts stop after GEMM2 (`do_finalize=False`) and hand an `UnfinalizedMoEOutput` to a consumer that fuses the top-k reduction into its own kernel. On `main`, a layer asks for this by setting `FusedMoEConfig.defer_moe_finalize`, optionally capped by `defer_moe_finalize_max_num_tokens`. This PR brings the same mechanism to the modular path, which models with their own router use (DeepSeek-V4.1's MXFP4 MoE, for one).

- **Experts.** `TrtLlmMxfp4ExpertsModular`, `TrtLlmNvFp4ExpertsModular` and `TrtLlmFp8ExpertsModular` (block FP8 and MXFP8) return the unfinalized output when `moe_config.should_defer_moe_finalize(M)` holds. `TrtLlmBf16ExpertsModular` is left out: it only runs with all2all kernels, which never defer.
- **Requested through a method.** Layers call `moe_config.defer_moe_finalize(max_num_tokens=-1)` instead of assigning the flag and the cap; the flag becomes private. Kimi-K3's runner moves to it, with the same behavior. A layer requests deferral only after checking that its quant method's `experts_cls` is one of these TRTLLM-Gen experts, as Kimi-K3 already does; other experts ignore the request. Deferral also now requires `hidden_dim == hidden_dim_unpadded`, since a consumer can't strip hidden-dim padding from GEMM2 rows.
- **The request is a hint; `should_defer_moe_finalize(M)` is the answer.** Each launch permutes into its own buffer, so a call the MXFP4 or NVFP4 experts would split across launches can't be deferred. When built, those experts lower `defer_moe_finalize_max_num_tokens` to their single-launch size. A call above it finalizes as before, and `should_defer_moe_finalize(M)` returns `False` for it. The model asks before calling and takes the matching path, so it never gets an output form it didn't expect. For DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash's MXFP4 experts (384 experts, top-k 6), that single-launch size is 86,868 tokens.
- **Modular kernel.** `FusedMoEKernelModularImpl` passes the unfinalized output through and skips `finalize`, but only when `prepare_finalize.supports_deferred_moe_finalize()` holds. That method moves up from the monolithic prepare/finalize base to `FusedMoEPrepareAndFinalize`. `MoEPrepareAndFinalizeNoDPEPModular` opts in, since its `finalize` is only the top-k weight-and-reduce.
- **Types.** `FusedMoEKernel.apply` now returns `torch.Tensor | UnfinalizedMoEOutput`, like `apply_monolithic`. So do `FusedMoEMethodBase.apply`, `RoutedExperts.forward_modular`, and the `apply` of each quant method whose oracle can pick one of these experts.

No layer requests deferral for modular experts yet, and Kimi-K3 behaves as before, so this changes no behavior on its own. The first consumer is #58586 (DSV4.1: MoE finalize fused into the TP all-reduce + mHC boundary), which will be restacked on this PR.

**Duplicate check.** #52601 (MiniMax-M3 MoE tail all-reduce fusion; last updated 2026-09-02) carries the same modular-kernel pass-through, NoDPEP opt-in and NVFP4 modular deferral, next to its model-specific tail. This PR splits out the shared part and adds the MXFP4 and FP8 experts and the `FusedMoEKernel.apply` return type, with no consumer, so #52601 and #58586 can both rebase onto it. No other open PR touches modular-path deferral.

## Test Plan

On GB300 (SM103), FlashInfer 0.7.0 (`main`'s pin), torch 2.13.0+cu130:

- New tests share `check_deferred_moe_finalize` in `tests/kernels/moe/utils.py`. Each builds the kernel for one rank of a TP group, as production does, and runs it. It then calls `defer_moe_finalize()` with no token cap and runs it again, checking three things:
  - the deferred output, reduced with `moe_unpermute` (TRT-LLM's finalize kernel), equals the first run's output bit for bit;
  - modular experts hand back the router's FP32 weights unchanged;
  - for MXFP4 and NVFP4, a forced chunked run finalizes, bit-identical to the non-deferred run, and `should_defer_moe_finalize` reports it.
  - `tests/kernels/moe/test_ocp_mx_moe.py::test_trtllm_mxfp4_deferred_finalize` (modular, plus one monolithic case)
  - `tests/kernels/moe/test_trtllm_nvfp4_moe.py::test_trtllm_fp4_moe_deferred_finalize`
  - `tests/kernels/moe/test_flashinfer.py::test_trtllm_fp8_block_moe_deferred_finalize` (block FP8 and MXFP8)
- Regression: `tests/kernels/moe/test_trtllm_nvfp4_moe.py`, `test_flashinfer.py`, `test_trtllm_bf16_moe.py`, `test_modular_oai_triton_moe.py` and `test_ocp_mx_moe.py`, minus the two kernel sweeps that call FlashInfer directly. Also `tests/model_executor/test_flashinfer_autotune_warmup.py` and `tests/models/kimi_k3/test_latent_moe_tail.py::test_deferred_finalize_enabled_before_moe_kernel_setup`.
- `pre-commit run` on the changed files (ruff, typos, SPDX, forbidden imports, test tethering, mypy 3.10), and `pre-commit run mypy-3.12 --hook-stage manual`.

## Test Result

- New tests: 11/11 passed (MXFP4 modular ×3 and monolithic ×1, NVFP4 ×3, FP8 ×4 across block FP8 and MXFP8). The deferred output reduces to FlashInfer's own finalized output bit for bit in every case, and forced chunked runs finalize as `should_defer_moe_finalize` reports.
- Regression: all passed except failures that also occur on `main` (36f94d5fe8) on the same stack:
  - `test_trtllm_fp4_moe_no_graph` at the 704/4096 shapes, and with RELU² at 2048/1536, misses `atol=rtol=0.2` on 2–21 elements, out of up to 262144, against the torch reference.
  - `test_modular_oai_triton_moe.py` raises `NotImplementedError: Must use persistent kernel and be TMA-compliant for native MXFP` from triton_kernels on SM103.
- pre-commit (including mypy 3.10 and 3.12): passed.
- No model eval: nothing sets the knob for modular experts yet. #58586 will carry the DSV4.1 perf and accuracy results.

AI assistance (Claude Code) was used for this change and its tests.

commits.pr_title: [Perf][DSv4] Fuse inverse RoPE + FP8 quant into FlashInfer sparse MLA
commits.pr_body:
## Purpose

FlashInfer 0.7.0 (already pinned) ships the TRTLLM-GEN DSv4 sparse-MLA **RopeQuant** epilogue (flashinfer-ai/flashinfer#4918): the kernel applies the inverse RoPE to the attention output and casts it to FP8 with packed UE8M0 scales, in the layout DeepGEMM's `fp8_einsum` consumes. This PR uses it on `FLASHINFER_MLA_SPARSE_DSV4` for DeepSeek V4, so `wo_a` reads the kernel's FP8 output directly instead of a bf16 `[T, 128, 512]` output plus a separate `fused_inv_rope_fp8_quant` pass.

It mirrors the pattern the DSv4.1 FlashMLA mega-attention layer already uses (`_alloc_attn_out` returning a `QuantizedActivation` that `_o_proj` consumes whole).

### Changes
- `DeepseekV4Attention` gets an `_alloc_attn_out` hook. The default stays the padded bf16 buffer (still head-sliced before `_o_proj`), so the FlashMLA, SM120, ROCm, XPU and CPU layers are unchanged.
- `DeepseekV4FlashInferMLAAttention` allocates RopeQuant's buffers. `deep_gemm_fp8_o_proj` now also takes a `QuantizedActivation`: it skips `fused_inv_rope_fp8_quant` and feeds the kernel's FP8 output and scales straight to `fp8_einsum`.
- The launcher requires the output's group stride to equal `sum_q` (it has no stride field for O), so a token slice of a shared buffer is rejected. Both the decode and prefill calls therefore span the full, CUDA-graph-padded buffer and select their tokens through `cum_seq_lens_q`; the prefill call's offsets are not rebased. Rows outside `cum_seq_lens_q` are never read or written (checked with garbage pad rows under `CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING=1`).
- `build_flashinfer_mixed_sparse_indices` gains `num_rows` so it can size its outputs for those rows while computing only the real tokens.
- **DSpark non-causal decode (bugfix, affects the unfused path too).** The kernel treats every entry of its active index ranges as a key: the first `min(128, pos + 1)` columns (the query's causal SWA window) and `[128, sparse_topk_lens)`. `-1` is not skipped. DSpark's non-causal decode rows were copied in as one contiguous run with `sparse_topk_lens` set to the full row width. So the `-1` padding past the run was attended as keys, and with fewer than 128 context tokens the causal window also cut out the later block tokens. The builder now fills each row's causal window with the first visible entries, puts the rest from column 128 on, and sets `sparse_topk_lens` to exactly that. Every draft token then sees the whole block at any context length. Because the decode call passes real `seq_lens`, RopeQuant's derived positions match `positions` for the draft too. This is the DSv4 counterpart of #57432, which fixed the same two problems for DSv4.1 only; DSv4 reads neither of the metadata fields it added. #57432 presents each draft token as its own sequence with the full request length. RopeQuant cannot use that, because it derives RoPE positions from `seq_lens`. So this change keeps the real `seq_lens` and lays out each row around the query's causal window instead.

### When it is on
Automatically, with no flag, when all of these hold:
- exactly 128 local query heads (DSv4-Pro at TP1 or with DP attention). The kernel has one fixed 128-head schedule; padding fewer heads up to 128 measured slower;
- per-tensor FP8 KV cache;
- FP8 `wo_a`.

DSv4 has 8 heads per `wo_a` group at every TP size, so 128 local heads always means the kernel's 16 × 8 layout. That is DSv4-Pro at TP1 or with DP attention; Pro at TP2–16 and Flash have fewer heads and keep the existing path.

This includes the non-causal DSpark draft. The one inexact case is a draft block running past `max_model_len`: the draft clamps its positions there and RopeQuant does not reproduce the clamp, which only affects those drafts.

Everything else keeps the existing path.

## Not a duplicate
I searched open and closed PRs for RopeQuant, `dsv4_inv_rope_cos_sin_cache`, flashinfer#4918, and fused inverse-RoPE/FP8 on `FLASHINFER_MLA_SPARSE_DSV4`. No PR wires this epilogue into vLLM. The nearby DSv4 PRs (#57679 query RMSNorm+MXFP8, #57977 MXFP8 activations between DeepGEMM kernels, #55459 indexer Hadamard) touch different paths. #57432 (merged) fixed the DSpark non-causal FlashInfer layout for DSv4.1 only; the DSv4 fix here is the counterpart, done differently so RopeQuant can apply (see Changes).

## Test Plan
- **Unit (new):**
  - `test_flashinfer_rope_quant_matches_unfused_o_proj` runs one mixed step (two decodes, a three-token prefill, and three CUDA-graph pad rows) through the real `_forward` + `_o_proj`, fused and unfused, and compares the `wo_a` output.
  - `test_flashinfer_dspark_noncausal_block_sees_future_tokens[0|20|127|900]` runs a DSpark non-causal block (q_len 4) through the DSv4 layer. It checks each draft token against a reference over its full visible set (context window plus the whole block), then checks that the fused output projects like the unfused one. Without the fix it fails at both contexts it was run at (20, 900); the kernel probe below shows the old layout off at every context tried.
- **Existing suites:**
  - `.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/kernels/attention/test_flashmla_sparse.py`
  - `.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/v1/attention/test_dspark_noncausal_sparse_mla.py`
  - `.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/v1/attention/test_deepseek_v4_swa_visible.py`
  - `.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/kernels/test_fused_inv_rope_fp8_quant.py`
- **Kernel microbenchmark** (standalone script, not included): decode under CUDA graphs, fused vs bf16 attention + `fused_inv_rope_fp8_quant`, on 1×GB300.
- **E2E accuracy A/B**, as described in the results below.
- `pre-commit run` on the changed files, including mypy.

## Test Result
**Tests:** all pass on GB300. `test_flashmla_sparse` 19/19, `test_dspark_noncausal_sparse_mla` 33 passed and 8 skipped, `test_deepseek_v4_swa_visible` 28/28, `test_fused_inv_rope_fp8_quant` 82/82 (on the first commit). pre-commit passes. The suites ran on a checkout of the parent commit (09fe178dba) plus this change; none of the 12 commits between it and the branch base touch these files.

**Kernel probe for the index layout:** FlashInfer called directly with a 4-token block per request, compared with a torch reference over the full visible set. With per-token split rows the max error is 0.008–0.029 at contexts 0, 1, 20, 100, 126, 127, 128 and 900, the same level as ordinary causal rows (0.008–0.02). The old contiguous rows are off by 0.09–0.6 at every context.

**E2E accuracy** (first commit; no DSpark), DeepSeek-V4-Pro-0813, DEP8 over 2×4 GB300 (tp 1 per rank, so 128 local heads), `--attention-config.backend FLASHINFER_MLA_SPARSE_DSV4 --kv-cache-dtype fp8`, MegaMoE. The two arms are identical except that the baseline loads a clean worktree of the same HEAD. The fused arm logged `fuses the inverse RoPE and FP8 quant` on every node; the baseline did not.

| | fused (this PR) | baseline |
|---|---|---|
| gsm8k 5-shot greedy, completions (n=1319), flexible / strict | 0.9530 / 0.9538 | 0.9545 / 0.9553 |
| aime25 ×4, temperature 1.0, max_tokens 98304 (n=120), exact_match | 0.9667 | 0.9833 |
| aime25 pass@4 | 1.0 | 1.0 |
| request errors | 0 | 0 |

The gsm8k gap is 2 of 1319 questions, inside greedy batching noise. The aime25 gap is 2 of 120 samples at temperature 1.0, and both arms solve every problem at least once.

**E2E with DSpark** (the index-layout fix plus RopeQuant on the draft), same setup plus `--speculative-config '{"method":"dspark","num_speculative_tokens":7,"draft_sample_method":"greedy"}'`. The baseline is the same clean worktree (old layout, unfused). Acceptance comes from `vllm:spec_decode_*` snapshots on both nodes around each eval, and per-position acceptance from the whole run.

| | fused (this PR) | baseline |
|---|---|---|
| gsm8k flexible / strict | 0.9538 / 0.9545 | 0.9553 / 0.9560 |
| gsm8k acceptance length (rate) | **4.42** (0.489) | 3.70 (0.386) |
| aime25 ×4 exact_match, pass@4 | 0.9917, 1.0 | 0.9833, 1.0 |
| aime25 acceptance length (rate) | **3.83** (0.405) | 3.31 (0.330) |
| whole-run per-position acceptance, 0 → 6 | 0.796, 0.632, 0.490, 0.371, 0.276, 0.189, 0.115 | 0.774, 0.585, 0.402, 0.264, 0.168, 0.096, 0.044 |

- Acceptance length rises 19.5% on gsm8k and 15.9% on aime25, in line with the +20% #57432 measured for the same fix on DSv4.1.
- Every draft position gains, and the gain grows with depth, from +3% at position 0 to 2.6× at position 6.
- Accuracy is unchanged within noise: gsm8k differs by 2 of 1319, and aime25 by 1 of 120 at temperature 1.0.

**Serving perf, 8k in / 1k out**: DeepSeek-V4-Pro-0813, DEP4 on one GB300 node (4 DP ranks at tp 1, so 128 local heads), `FLASHINFER_MLA_SPARSE_DSV4`, FP8 KV, MegaMoE, no speculative decoding. The two arms run the same config and differ only in the vLLM tree. The benchmark is a closed-loop `vllm-bench` sweep: exact token ids, `--ignore-eos`, 10 requests per slot, prefix cache reset between points. The arms ran concurrently on two different nodes, so low-concurrency TTFT is not comparable; ITL p50 is.

| concurrency | output tok/s/GPU, fused / base (Δ) | TPOT p50 ms (Δ) | ITL p50 ms (Δ) | TTFT p50 ms | ITL p99 ms |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 19.0 / 19.4 (−1.9%) | 12.73 / 12.43 (+2.5%) | 12.70 / 12.39 (+2.5%) | 494 / 549 | 13.1 / 12.7 |
| 2 | 34.7 / 35.2 (−1.3%) | 13.38 / 13.09 (+2.2%) | 13.31 / 13.02 (+2.2%) | 597 / 1050 | 13.7 / 13.4 |
| 4 | 63.3 / 63.9 (−0.8%) | 14.64 / 14.37 (+1.8%) | 14.24 / 13.94 (+2.2%) | 1108 / 1212 | 14.7 / 14.4 |
| 16 | **213.3 / 183.8 (+16.0%)** | 17.57 / 19.19 (−8.4%) | 16.99 / 17.12 (−0.7%) | 1370 / 2631 | 17.8 / 18.0 |
| 64 | **444.7 / 417.5 (+6.5%)** | 33.28 / 35.29 (−5.7%) | 23.80 / 24.42 (−2.5%) | 3468 / 3649 | 68.0 / 490.5 |
| 256 | **853.3 / 783.3 (+8.9%)** | 70.50 / 77.70 (−9.3%) | 34.94 / 35.56 (−1.8%) | 3597 / 4329 | 909.5 / 1180.2 |

- **One request per rank (c1–c4):** the decode step is 2–2.5% slower. This is the kernel's fixed cost at batch 1 per rank with long KV, the same corner as in the kernel table below.
- **c16 and up:** most of the gain is in prefill, not the decode step (ITL p50 improves only 0.7–2.5%).
  - With 8k prompts, the unfused path writes and re-reads a bf16 `[8192, 128, 512]` attention output per layer before quantizing it; RopeQuant removes that.

commits.pr_title: [Bugfix] Stop leaking the internal field name in the max_tokens validation error
commits.pr_body:
## Purpose

`TokenizeParams.__post_init__` builds the "output tokens exceed the context length" message with the
f-string self-documenting specifier:

```python
f"{self.max_total_tokens_param}={max_total_tokens=}. "
```

`{max_total_tokens=}` expands to `max_total_tokens=<value>` on its own, so the public override name
is emitted and then immediately followed by the *internal attribute name*. A deployment that remaps
the name — which the field exists to allow ("Override this to edit the message for validation
errors") — produces:

```
max_tokens=20000 cannot be greater than max_model_len=max_total_tokens=8192.
```

`max_total_tokens` is an internal field: it is not a request body field and not a server flag
(`--max-model-len` is the user-facing one). So the 400 error tells the client about a name it cannot
set, and the doubled `name=name=` looks like a formatting bug even when the remapping is the default.

Reproduced directly: constructing `TokenizeParams(max_total_tokens=8192, max_output_tokens=20000)`
before the fix yields `... cannot be greater than max_total_tokens=max_total_tokens=8192.`

## Fix

Drop the trailing `=` so the value is interpolated plainly. This matches the sibling truncation
message a few lines below (`vllm/renderers/params.py:250`), which already writes
`{max_input_tokens}` without the specifier — so the corrected form is the one the file uses
elsewhere, not a new convention.

## Test plan

Added `tests/renderers/test_params_validation.py`:

- `test_max_output_error_uses_public_name_once` — remaps both parameter names, asserts the message
  reads `max_tokens=20000 cannot be greater than max_model_len=8192` and that the string
  `max_total_tokens` does **not** appear anywhere in it.
- `test_max_output_error_with_default_names` — pins the default-name rendering so the fix cannot
  simply delete the value.

Verified locally on an editable install of `main`:

| check | result |
|---|---|
| with the fix | 2 passed |
| fix reverted | the first test **fails** |
| `ruff-check`, `ruff-format`, `typos`, `check-spdx-header`, `check-test-tethering` | all pass |

Only the message text changes; no signature, no control flow, no behavior a client can depend on
other than the error string itself.

commits.pr_title: [Frontend] Handle Disable Thinking in /v1/messages
commits.pr_body:
ORIGINAL CREDIT TO: [jryberg](https://github.com/jryberg) --- will make you co-author if you don't reply :)

## Purpose

`AnthropicMessagesRequest` never declared a `thinking` field, so `/v1/messages` silently dropped the documented Anthropic parameter (Pydantic's default `extra="ignore"`). Clients asking for disabled thinking or a token budget got whatever `output_config.effort` implied.

This matters for Claude Code in particular: its client-side auto-mode classifier (`CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_MODE_SERVER=0`) sends `thinking: {"type": "disabled"}` with `max_tokens: 64` and `stop_sequences: ["</severity>"]`, and expects `<severity>N` right away. On reasoning models the template kept thinking on, so the classifier used its whole budget reasoning and never produced a verdict.

### Changes

- `protocol.py`: add `AnthropicThinkingConfig` (`type: enabled | disabled | adaptive`, `budget_tokens`, `display`) and a `thinking` field on `AnthropicMessagesRequest`.
- `serving.py`: add `_handle_thinking`, which runs after `_handle_output_config` so an explicit `thinking` overrides the effort-derived default:

  | `thinking` | maps to |
  |---|---|
  | `{"type": "disabled"}` | `reasoning_effort = <disabled effort>` (see below) |
  | `{"type": "enabled", "budget_tokens": N}` | `thinking_token_budget = N` |
  | `{"type": "enabled"}` (no budget) | nothing |
  | `{"type": "adaptive"}` | nothing; `output_config.effort` stays the ceiling |
  | `display` | accepted, ignored |

- `display` is ignored on purpose. Mapping `"omitted"` to `include_reasoning=False` would mark reasoning as ended for structured outputs and drop it from multi-turn history. Reasoning is always returned.
- New flag `--anthropic-disabled-thinking-effort {auto,none,minimal,low,medium,high,xhigh,max}` (default `auto`) sets the `reasoning_effort` used for `thinking.type=disabled`:
  - `none` turns thinking off on templates that support it.
  - `low` is for models that always think (e.g. GLM-5.3) or that reject `none` (e.g. gpt-oss).
  - `auto` checks the chat template on the first disabled-thinking request and caches the result. It renders a probe prompt with `reasoning_effort="none"` and falls back to `low` if the renderer rejects `none` or renders the same prompt as some thinking effort (e.g. GLM-5.3 treats unknown efforts as `max`). Otherwise it uses `none`. The chosen value is logged once at INFO.
- `count_tokens` requests are unaffected.

### Relationship to other PRs

This combines two open PRs so that one of them can land:

- #53058 (@jryberg): the original `thinking` field and mapping. This PR keeps that commit (with authorship) and changes two things: `display` is no longer mapped to `include_reasoning`, and the disabled-thinking effort is now configurable or auto-detected instead of always being `"none"`.
- #58448 (mine): the same fix for `thinking.type=disabled`, driven by the Claude Code auto-mode classifier. It set `enable_thinking=False` directly. That approach is replaced here by the `reasoning_effort` mapping, which also works for templates that don't read `enable_thinking`.

If this lands, I'll close #58448, and #53058 can be closed as superseded.

## Test Plan

```bash
.venv/bin/python -m pytest \
  tests/entrypoints/anthropic/test_anthropic_messages_conversion.py \
  tests/entrypoints/anthropic/test_protocol_exports.py -v
```

New tests:
- `TestThinkingConfig`: absent `thinking` changes nothing. `disabled` sets `reasoning_effort` and overrides `output_config.effort`. `enabled` with a budget sets `thinking_token_budget`. `enabled` without a budget and `adaptive` pin nothing. A configured disabled effort is honored. `display` leaves reasoning included. A captured Claude Code payload converts correctly.
- `TestProbeDisabledThinkingEffort`: `auto` resolves to `none` when the template honors it, and to `low` when the template ignores effort, renders `none` the same as a thinking effort, or the renderer rejects `none`.

## Test Result

```
71 passed, 14 warnings in 11.97s
```

This PR was written with AI assistance (Claude Code), and I reviewed and tested it. The base commit from #53058 was also AI-assisted, as its author disclosed.

commits.pr_title: [Structured Outputs] Parse Lark grammars natively in the xgrammar backend
commits.pr_body:
## Purpose

`structured_outputs.grammar` accepts either EBNF or Lark. The xgrammar backend handled Lark with vLLM's hand-written `convert_lark_to_ebnf`, which ran during frontend validation and rewrote the request's grammar in place. It has two problems:

- It does not handle common Lark features such as regex terminals (`/[0-9]+/`), `%import common.LF`, and rule aliases (`-> name`). For example, Codex's `apply_patch` custom-tool grammar fails with `Referenced rules are not defined: LF, line`.
- It accepts input that is not Lark, such as single-quoted literals or a grammar without a `start` rule.

XGrammar (0.2.7, the pinned version) parses Lark natively with `Grammar.from_lark` and `GrammarCompiler.compile_lark`. This PR uses them instead:

- **Validation** (`validate_xgrammar_grammar`) picks Lark or EBNF with the existing `grammar_is_likely_lark` check. It only parses and no longer rewrites the request.
- **Compilation** (`XgrammarBackend.compile_grammar`) makes the same choice, so a Lark grammar also compiles when the request was not validated by the Python frontend.
- **Removal:** `convert_lark_to_ebnf` is deleted.

This matches the guidance backend, where `llguidance.grammar_from("grammar", ...)` also decides between Lark and GBNF itself.

**Behavior change:** grammars that only the old converter accepted, such as `start: 'a'` or `rule: "hello"` without `start`, are now rejected with the existing "Invalid grammar specification." validation error. Lark itself and the guidance backend reject them too.

**Relation to #57695:** that open PR makes quote handling in `convert_lark_to_ebnf` escape-aware. This PR removes the converter and delegates to XGrammar's native Lark parser, so it would supersede that change.

## Test Plan

```bash
pytest -q tests/v1/structured_output/test_backend_xgrammar_lark.py
pytest -q tests/v1/structured_output/
```

The new `test_backend_xgrammar_lark.py` (a `cpu_test`) covers:
- validation accepts Lark and EBNF without rewriting the grammar;
- the `auto` backend selects xgrammar for Lark;
- invalid Lark (missing `start`, single-quoted literals) is rejected;
- compiled Lark and EBNF grammars accept and reject the same inputs;
- Lark features: a regex terminal, `%import common`, and a rule alias.

## Test Result

- The new tests with this PR: 10 passed.

commits.pr_title: [MM] Add Triton kernel for mm_input_normal.
commits.pr_body:
## Purpose `mm_input_norm` is a memory-bandwidth-bound operator: one multiply-add per element, so runtime is dominated by DRAM traffic. This PR adds a Triton fusion kernel that performs the whole per-channel affine transform in a single pass, replacing the eager path that materialized an fp32 intermediate. The Triton fused kernel is **significantly faster** than the eager, `BatchNorm1d`, and `torch.compile` baselines on the same workload, because it reads the input once and writes the output once — no intermediate DRAM round-trip. https://github.com/noooop/snippet/tree/main/kernel_bench/mm_input_normal This basically saturates my local 4090's VRAM bandwidth ～850GB/s. ``` ./nvbandwidth -t device_local_copy_sm -b 1024 Running device_local_copy_sm. memcpy SM local GPU(column) bandwidth (GB/s) 0 0 1695.46 SUM device_local_copy_sm 1695.46 ``` 1. **Single-pass fusion** — `y = x * weight[c] + bias[c]` computed in one kernel launch, at the input's native dtype (`uint8`/`fp16`/`bf16`/`fp32`). 2. **Preallocated output** — the caller can pass a larger buffer; only the `[:N]` region is written, so buffers can be reused across calls without a per-call allocation. 3. **`float32` compute for free** — arithmetic is done in fp32 inside the kernel regardless of I/O dtypes. This matches the eager path numerically but costs no bandwidth, since the intermediate never leaves registers. ## Test Plan pytest tests/models/multimodal/generation_ppl_test/test_qwen.py pytest tests/model_executor/layers/test_mm_input_norm.py ## Test Result pass ---

commits.pr_title: [Qwen4Exp][ROCm] PLE n-gram table CPU offload
commits.pr_body:
## Purpose
- Enable `VLLM_PLE_CPU_OFFLOAD` on the AMD/ROCm path: keep the Qwen4Exp PLE n-gram table in pinned host memory, read through a UVA view on the GPU.
- Free VRAM so `Qwen/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-FP8` (FP8 table ~51 GiB) / `Inferact/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4` (bf16 table ~102 GiB) serve on one MI300X with the table entirely in host RAM.
- Keep the pinned lookup behind a custom op (`qwen4_exp_amd_ple_ngram_embedding_pinned`) with `mutates_args=["output"]` so the large embedding weight is never materialized by `torch.compile` (Inductor autotuning builds a bf16 copy of the table during compile, which OOMs on AMD setups without enough VRAM) and the op survives aot_autograd/Inductor.
- Move the PLE embedding storage classes to `qwen4_exp/common` so the AMD and NVIDIA paths share one implementation (NVIDIA re-exports).
- Relax the PLE enable gate to `is_cuda_alike()` so ROCm is accepted, matching the existing NVIDIA default (`VLLM_PLE_CPU_OFFLOAD` defaults on for both; `=0` opts out). Also, my local testing shows little to no performance loss for PLE offload while saving a good chunk of VRAM for more KV cache.
- Why this is not duplicating existing PRs: 
  - #54371 (merged — source of the UVA offload code, ported here)
  - #55040 (AMD FP8 PLE, different approach: FP8 storage + forward dequant vs load-time bf16 fold; no offload/prefetch)
  - #55334 / #54070 / #54129 (nvidia + mmap — complementary).

commits.pr_title: [CI][ROCm] Prevent Model Executor apt stalls
commits.pr_body:
- Bake `libsodium23` into the ROCm, gfx1250, and TheRock `ci_base` stages, which already inherit `curl`.
- Remove runtime apt installation from the legacy AMD Model Executor job and override the shared job's AMD commands to use the image dependencies.
- Add three native apt download retries and 30-second HTTP/HTTPS connection and inactivity timeouts to the affected `ci_base` update and install commands.
- Limit index updates to five minutes, with a 30-second grace period before forced termination, and use `--error-on=any` to stop installation after an incomplete update.

AMD Model Executor jobs were spending their test budget fetching apt indexes before pytest could start.
The [Model Executor log](https://buildkite.com/vllm/amd-ci/builds/11263/list?jid=019f9aea-adb1-449b-ab2a-d0cb1dfcbed8&tab=output) from [AMD CI build #11263](https://buildkite.com/vllm/amd-ci/builds/11263) shows an update stalling during Ubuntu index retrieval until cancellation roughly three hours later. The reported seven-day review found 28 similar stalls across 25 nodes, with many jobs consuming approximately an hour without reaching package installation or tests. Baking the dependencies into `ci_base` removes this recurring network dependency from the AMD test jobs, while bounded retries let the image build recover from transient download failures or fail promptly when they persist.

commits.pr_title: [Perf][Distributed] Add low-SM multimem reduce-scatter for SM100/SM103
commits.pr_body:
## Purpose

Add a low-SM MNNVL reduce-scatter backend for TP2, TP4, and TP8 MNNVL groups on SM100 or SM103. The kernel uses `multimem.ld_reduce` to reduce across the NVLS multicast mapping and ordinary local stores for each rank-owned output shard. It launches at most 8 CTAs per GPU with 1024 threads and an 8-way vector unroll.

The dispatcher uses total input message bytes and keeps a single explicit backend policy:

- `<= 16 MiB`: existing MNNVL Lamport reduce-scatter.
- `> 16 MiB` and `<= 64 MiB`: multimem reduce-scatter when its gate passes.
- `> 64 MiB`: return `None` to the existing NCCL reduce-scatter fallback.

The multimem gate requires TP2, TP4, or TP8, exact SM100 or SM103, BF16/FP16/FP32, valid 16-byte shard alignment, a group-spanning NVLS multicast mapping, and non-batch-invariant execution. Unsupported topology, architecture, dtype, alignment, mapping initialization, and message size all fail closed to the existing fallback.

The 64 MiB symmetric staging buffer is allocated lazily on the first eligible reduce-scatter. All ranks reduce their local allocation result before entering symmetric-memory rendezvous, so a failure on one rank makes the whole group fall back without stranding peers.

The 64 MiB upper cutoff is deliberately below the measured hot-cache crossover near 76 MiB and bounds the added symmetric staging allocation. Production-path timings include the staging copy and required barriers and report the median maximum-rank CUDA event time on 8x B300:

| Input size | Multimem, 8 CTA | NCCL | Multimem vs. NCCL |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 64 MiB, hot | 137.38 us | 148.83 us | 7.7% faster |
| 64 MiB, cold L2 | 141.18 us | 150.27 us | 6.0% faster |
| 76 MiB, hot | 161.79 us | 162.21 us | 0.3% faster |
| 96 MiB, hot | 198.53 us | 180.67 us | 9.9% slower |

A reusable multi-rank benchmark is included under `benchmarks/kernels/` and checks every eager and captured workspace against an FP32 distributed reference before timing.

This does not duplicate an existing contribution. Open PR and issue searches for SM100/SM103, multimem, custom all-reduce, and reduce-scatter found no implementation of this path. #50182 only adjusts symmetric-memory multicast selection, #44080 adjusts sequence-parallel fusion limits, and #53852 adds a FlashInfer all-reduce cutoff override.

## Test Plan

```bash

.venv/bin/python -m pytest \
```

commits.pr_title: [ROCm] Cut 69 wasted contiguous copies per decode step from the skinny GEMM path
commits.pr_body:
## Summary

`rocm_unquantized_gemm_impl` hoists a contiguous copy above the two branches
that consume it:

```python
if use_skinny:
    x_view = x.reshape(-1, x.size(-1)).contiguous()      # always runs
    if (m == 1 or m > 8) and 0 < n <= 5:
        return wvSplitK(..., x_view, ...)                # uses it
    elif m % 4 == 0 and n == 1 and k <= 8192 and bias is None:
        return LLMM1(..., x_view, ...)                   # uses it
    # neither matched -> fall through

if rocm_aiter_ops.is_tgemm_enabled():
    return tgemm.mm(x, weight, bias)                     # uses ORIGINAL x
return torch.nn.functional.linear(x, weight, bias)       # uses ORIGINAL x
```

The outer `use_skinny` gate is broad — ROCm gfx9/gfx11, fp16/bf16,
`k % 8 == 0` — while the inner conditions are narrow (`0 < n <= 5`, or
`n == 1`). Any shape that passes the gate and matches neither builds `x_view`,
discards it, and falls through to a path that uses the original `x`.

This moves the copy into the two branches that use it. The discarded value is
dead, so every path that consumed `x_view` still receives exactly the same
tensor.

## Results

Kimi-K3 FP4, 8x MI355X, TP8, concurrency 1, MTP depth 6, 384K-token context.
The layer that hits this is `f_b_proj` at **m=7, n=1536, k=128**: `k % 8 == 0`
passes the gate, `(m == 1 or m > 8)` is false, `m % 4 == 0` is false. Its input
is a 128-column slice of a 6284-wide projection output, so it is row-strided
and the copy is real work rather than a no-op.

BF16 `direct_copy_kernel_cuda`, same image and context, 6-step decode window:

| | per step | cost |
|---:|---:|---:|
| before | 73.0 | 0.3609 ms/step |
| after | 4.0 | 0.0218 ms/step |
| **removed** | **69.0** | **0.339 ms/step** |

69 removed per step is exactly one per KDA layer. Each moved 1,792 bytes for
about 4.8 us, so the cost was almost entirely launch overhead rather than
bandwidth. The 4 per step that remain are unrelated int64 index copies.

## How the copy was attributed

Not by reading the source — two earlier guesses from source were wrong. The
evidence is from profiles:

1. The kernel template is `gpu_kernel_impl_nocast<...(c10::BFloat16)>`, i.e. a
   same-dtype layout copy, not a dtype cast.
2. Fingerprinting neighbours in the kernel timeline put 420 of 438 copies
   directly between two Tensile GEMMs.
3. Re-running with CUDA graphs disabled kept all 438 copies, so they are not
   inserted by compilation. Every one then resolves through its `cpu_op`
   parents to:

   ```
   aten::copy_ <- aten::clone <- aten::contiguous <- vllm::rocm_unquantized_gemm
   ```

   414 of 414 attributed, 69 per step.
4. The control-flow arithmetic on the actual shape confirms both inner
   branches are false, so the copy is discarded.

A competing hypothesis — that Inductor inserted the copy because the custom op
carries no layout tag — was tested on GPU by tagging the op
`torch.Tag.flexible_layout`, and rejected: the count stayed at 73.0 per step.

## Correctness

No FLOPs change and no numerics change. The removed value was never read on
the affected path; on the two paths that do read it, the same
`x.reshape(-1, x.size(-1)).contiguous()` is still evaluated before use.

```
ruff check vllm/model_executor/layers/utils.py       All checks passed!
ruff format --check vllm/model_executor/layers/utils.py   1 file already formatted
```

## Why this is not a duplicate

```
gh pr list --repo vllm-project/vllm --state open --search "rocm_unquantized_gemm"
gh pr list --repo vllm-project/vllm --state open --search "skinny gemm contiguous"
gh pr list --repo vllm-project/vllm --state open --search "wvSplitK contiguous copy"
gh pr list --repo vllm-project/vllm --state open --search "rocm unquantized gemm x_view"
```

No open PR touches this function.

## Who is affected

No flag changes are needed to pick this up. `VLLM_ROCM_USE_SKINNY_GEMM`
defaults to `True`, so a stock ROCm deployment is already on the affected
path; the configuration measured above sets nothing related to it.

The waste occurs when the broad outer gate passes and both narrow inner
conditions miss:

| condition | |
| --- | --- |
| `VLLM_ROCM_USE_SKINNY_GEMM` | default `True` |
| `on_gfx9() or on_gfx1x()` | true on gfx950 (MI355X) |
| `x.dtype in [fp16, bf16]` | true for these activations |
| `k % 8 == 0` | 128 % 8 == 0 |
| `skinny_operands_compatible` | contiguous weight and bias |
| **inner:** `(m == 1 or m > 8) and 0 < n <= 5` | **false** at m=7, n=1536 |
| **inner:** `m % 4 == 0 and n == 1 and ...` | **false** at m=7, n=1536 |

Two consequences worth stating plainly, so the scope is not overread:

- A model whose GEMM shapes *do* match an inner branch was always consuming
  `x_view`, so there is nothing to remove and no change is expected.
- Anyone running with `VLLM_ROCM_USE_SKINNY_GEMM=0` never entered this block
  and is unaffected.

The copy is only real work when the input is non-contiguous. Here it is: the
`f_b_proj` input is a 128-column slice of a 6284-wide projection output. A
shape that passes the gate with an already-contiguous input pays a cheaper
no-op rather than a full copy.

## End-to-end (side note)

Deliberately last, and not the claim being made. 0.339 ms/step is roughly 1.5%
of a 23.5 ms decode step at this operating point, which is close to the
run-to-run spread we measure on this workload (~0.8%), and end-to-end
throughput also depends on the tuning of the surrounding GEMMs and attention
kernels. The removed copy count above is the honest result.

The benefit is not specific to Kimi-K3: any ROCm model whose GEMM shapes pass
the `use_skinny` gate while missing both inner conditions pays this today.

---

run by the submitter on MI355X hardware, and every changed line was reviewed by
the submitter.

commits.pr_title: [Bugfix][Quantization] Fix MXFP8 startup crash on layers below mm_mxfp8 shape limits
commits.pr_body:
## Purpose

`vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3.5-0.8B --quantization mxfp8` dies in the profile run on a B200 with `AssertionError: mm_mxfp8 requires N >= 128, got N=32`. The layer is the GDN `in_proj_ba` (weight 32 x 1024). The larger Qwen3.5 sizes and Qwen3-Next have N=64 or N=96 there, so the whole family fails to start with online MXFP8.

`FlashInferCutlassMxfp8LinearKernel` and `FlashInferCutedslMxfp8LinearKernel` return `True` from `can_implement` for every layer. The `mm_mxfp8` shape limits (N >= 128, K >= 128, K % 32 == 0) are only asserts inside `apply_weights`, so on SM100 a layer below the limits is still selected instead of falling through to Marlin.

`Mxfp8LinearLayerConfig` gains a two-element `(N, K)` `weight_shape`, and the two FlashInfer kernels share a shape validator called by `can_implement`. CUTLASS adds its SM12x-specific alignment check. The compressed-tensors, INC and online MXFP8 schemes select the kernel in `create_weights` instead of `__init__`, the per-layer pattern `Fp8LinearMethod` already uses. ModelOpt already selects in `create_weights` since #49381, so there this PR forwards the weight shape and extracts the trailing `(N, K)` dimensions at the BMM re-selection call site. No kernel code changes.

From @stecasta's review: on SM12x the CUTLASS kernel also rejects N % 32 != 0, and `MarlinMxfp8LinearKernel.can_implement` now rejects N <= 0, K <= 0 and K % 32 != 0.

On an L4 and an RTX PRO 6000 (SM120), the third passes for all five shapes, including the new (32, 256), (96, 256) and (130, 256). `pre-commit run` is clean on the changed files. The B200 run below is from the original base d1922cb5a; the rebase changed no kernel code.

commits.pr_title: [Perf][Engram] Serialize offloaded lookups and pack host tables into huge pages
commits.pr_body:
## Purpose

Two CPU-offloaded Engram lookups ran on separate streams and interfered with main-stream decoder work. Use one model-owned stream and a completion event per layer, so the lookups take turns instead of jointly starving decoder compute of SMs, and the first consumer waits only for its own lookup.

For private CPU-offloaded tables, `thp_packing` allocates weights and scales in one anonymous mapping that requests transparent huge pages (`MADV_HUGEPAGE`), prefaults it, and registers it with CUDA. Before prefaulting, the cached pages of the local checkpoint snapshot are released (`posix_fadvise(DONTNEED)`) so the kernel can find contiguous physical memory; after weight loading refills that cache, it is released again and one `MADV_COLLAPSE` is attempted. Huge pages are best effort: any failure falls back to ordinary Torch pinned memory or keeps the existing pages with a warning, and correctness never depends on them. Small tables, DP shared storage, the lookup kernel and the SM/2 background grid are unchanged.

Why the page-cache release and the post-load collapse are kept: measured on one GB200 NUMA node (441 GiB) with 250 GiB of small-page anonymous memory resident and the DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash checkpoint in the page cache, allocating a 25 GiB table:

| Step | Huge-page coverage |
|---|---|
| prefault, no fadvise | 12-22% |
| fadvise before prefault | 66% |
| + post-load fadvise + `MADV_COLLAPSE` | 100% |
| post-load collapse without fadvise | `ENOMEM`, unchanged |

`EngramConfig.thp_packing` defaults to `False`; set `--engram-config '{"thp_packing": true}'` to enable it. Page allocation follows the host's THP policy; the code does not change system settings.

Duplicate-work check (2026-09-15): [#56436](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/56436) controls overlap eligibility; [#56757](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/56757) uses file-backed tables. Neither serializes the offloaded lookups on a single model-owned stream nor implements this registered THP allocation path.

## Test plan

```bash
.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/kernels/test_engram.py \
  tests/distributed/test_engram_dp_shard.py -q
.venv/bin/pre-commit run --files \
  vllm/config/engram.py vllm/models/deepseek_v41/nvidia/engram.py \
  vllm/models/deepseek_v41/nvidia/model.py \
  tests/kernels/test_engram.py tests/test_config.py
.venv/bin/pre-commit run mypy-3.12 --hook-stage manual --files \
  vllm/config/engram.py vllm/models/deepseek_v41/nvidia/engram.py \
  vllm/models/deepseek_v41/nvidia/model.py \
  tests/kernels/test_engram.py
git diff --check
```

## Test result

- `tests/kernels/test_engram.py`: 86 passed, 1 skipped (GB200). New guards: packed storage and its pinned fallback give exact lookup rows; a passed-in stream is the lookup stream; consuming one layer does not wait for a later layer's lookup on the shared stream (fails with the previous stream-wide `wait_stream`).
- `tests/test_config.py -k engram`: 40 passed; `tests/distributed/test_engram_dp_shard.py`: 23 passed, 2 skipped.
- Pre-commit, `mypy-3.12`, and `git diff --check` passed.

## Model evaluation

GSM8K with lm-eval 0.4.12 (all 1319 problems, five-shot chat, greedy, 1024 output tokens, seed 123) on 4xGB200, TP4, eager, checkpoint `deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash@dba1be0a`:

| `thp_packing` | Accuracy |
| --- | --- |
| OFF | 96.51% (1273/1319) |
| ON | 96.59% (1274/1319) |

The ON run had all 8 tables fully huge-page backed (192 GiB, 100% coverage, no fallback). The two-problem delta is within run-to-run noise; THP packing changes only how table memory is backed, not its contents.

## Performance

E2E average TTFT (ms, lower is better), same serving config for all three variants. A = independent lookup streams + pinned tables; B = one serialized model-owned stream + pinned tables; C = serialized stream + THP-packed tables (this PR).

| Input / concurrency | A | B | C | C vs A | C vs B |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 8K / 1 | 230.88 | 237.16 | 229.53 | -0.58% | -3.22% |
| 8K / 32 | 1642.64 | 1617.62 | 1595.97 | -2.84% | -1.34% |
| 32K / 1 | 891.66 | 887.84 | 886.45 | -0.58% | -0.16% |
| 32K / 32 | 5160.91 | 5128.07 | 5104.18 | -1.10% | -0.47% |

C is fastest in every configuration; the gain grows with concurrency at 8K input (up to -2.84% vs A, -3.22% vs B at the opposite ends of the matrix).

Kernel-level comparison of the lookup itself (SM/2 background grid, one DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash TP4 shard: 96,002,653 rows x 256 fp8 + ue8m0 scales, ~24.8 GiB host table, CUPTI timing with CUDA graphs and cold L2, mean of 20 reps with rotated measurement order, THP coverage 97.4%):

| tokens / lookup | THP (us) | 64K pinned (us) | speedup |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 2.68 | 2.69 | 1.00x |
| 32 | 3.28 | 3.35 | 1.02x |
| 512 | 8.56 | 11.24 | 1.31x |
| 2048 | 28.30 | 34.26 | 1.21x |
| 8192 | 102.32 | 264.58 | 2.59x |
| 32768 | 392.51 | 3947.99 | 10.06x |

THP is at parity for decode-sized lookups and increasingly faster beyond 512 tokens: the 64 KiB baseline collapses to ~13 GB/s at 32K tokens from GPU MMU TLB thrash (unstable across runs, 2.8-41x), while THP sustains ~134 GB/s of host read bandwidth. An ablation with mmap+cudaHostRegister but no huge pages matched cudaHostAlloc at every size, so the difference comes from the page size alone, not the allocation path.

AI assistance was used for implementation, testing, and this draft. Human review of every changed line and independent execution of relevant tests are required before submission.

commits.pr_title: [Bugfix][Qwen4Exp] Keep pinned PLE prefetch ids out of the CUDA graph pool
commits.pr_body:
## Problem and fix

Fixes #58441. With `engram_config.cpu_offload=True`, `Qwen4ExpPLEPinnedHostEmbedding.start_prefetch` launches the PLE lookup on a side stream and returns; `_finalize_prefetch` joins it one decoder layer later. Qwen4Exp defaults to breakable CUDA graphs, so for PIECEWISE batches (prefill/mixed batches up to the capture size, or every batch with `cudagraph_mode=PIECEWISE`) `start_prefetch` is an eager break and its arguments are replaced by `weak_ref_tensor`s. Two things then combine:

- `gathered_ids.record_stream(prefetch_stream)` is a no-op: with `etp_data_parallel_size == 1`, `gathered_ids` is the weak ref itself, and the caching allocator skips `recordStream` for storage it does not own.
- The only strong reference to the ids is the local `ngram_ids` in `Qwen4ExpNGramEmbedding.start_prefetch`, which drops as soon as it returns, while the next segment is already being captured. The graph-pool block goes straight back to the free list and the rest of the preceding decoder layer can be captured on top of it.

At replay the side stream reads the ids while the main stream may be overwriting them, so greedy outputs silently stop being reproducible.

The fix computes the prefetch ids into a persistent per-layer buffer through the existing `output=` argument of `compute_ngram_ids`. This mirrors the persistent `_prefetch_buffer` already used for the lookup output, adds no kernel or copy, and costs `max_num_batched_tokens * ngram_heads * 8` bytes per PLE layer. FULL graphs and eager runs were already safe (the argument stays a real tensor there), and ETP spanning DP is unaffected (the ids are re-gathered into a fresh tensor inside the eager break).

## Validation

```bash
.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/models/qwen4_exp/test_ple.py -q
.venv/bin/pre-commit run --files tests/models/qwen4_exp/test_ple.py vllm/models/qwen4_exp/nvidia/ngram_embedding.py
```

- **51 passed** on GB200. The new `test_ngram_prefetch_ids_outlive_start_prefetch` reproduces the lifetime bug without a full graph capture: the prefetch stub keeps a weak ref to the ids, as the eager break does, and a fresh `MemPool` makes the next same-size allocation reuse freed storage, as a later graph segment would. On main the weak ref reads the overwritten `-1`s (3/3 runs); with this change it reads the reference ids.
- Pre-commit passed.
- No model eval: the ids are produced by the same kernel into a different buffer, so outputs only change where the race corrupted them. The reporter's cold/warm greedy table in #58441 (8/8 identical once the ids are in a persistent buffer) covers the end-to-end effect.

## Related work and AI assistance

Open-PR search found no equivalent fix. #57785 joins side-stream work during breakable capture and does not affect replay (row 2 of the table in #58441); #57497 and #58439 move or add PLE backends without changing this lifetime.
